headline: Omote is a compound of 面 (omo, “face”) plus 手 (te, “hand; direction, side”), basically meaning “face-wards; facing side”.
Yameru is from Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *yamu, and a doublet of 辞める (yameru, “to quit (a job)”).
Utsu is from Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *ut-.
Oto is from Old Japanese, and a rare geminate form otto appears in the late 1400s.
Asu is from Old Japanese, first attested in the Kojiki of 712, and several theories exist about its ultimate derivation.
Shimo is from Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *simo.
Jō is from Middle Chinese 上.
Sei is from Middle Chinese 生, in the kan'on reading, so likely a later borrowing.
Idaku is a shift from the earlier udaku.
Uru is from Old Japanese and first attested in about 759 in the Man'yōshū.
On is from Middle Chinese 音.
Kane is from Old Japanese, possibly derived from the unbound prefix kana- fused with い (i, nominal particle).
Kami is from Old Japanese and already apparent in the Kojiki (about 712) and the Man'yōshū (about 759).
Gara is an alteration of kara, and the kara changes to gara as an instance of rendaku (連濁).
Kyū is from Middle Chinese 毬/球 (“ball, sphere, orb”).
Kuda is from Old Japanese and first attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720.
Go is from Middle Chinese 後 (“after”).
Miyako is a compound of 宮 (miya, “imperial palace”) plus 処 (ko, “place”).
Myōgonichi is 明後 (myōgo-, “the ... after next ...”) plus 日 (nichi, “day”).
